section.title: Be Holy
section.sectionRationale: Having celebrated the living hope, Peter draws the first great therefore of the letter. The mercy just described now calls for a whole new way of life: minds set on grace, conduct marked by holiness and reverent fear, and love flowing from hearts reborn by God's enduring word. Indicative has become imperative; who they are becomes how they live.
section.thesis: Because they have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ and born again through the living word of God, believers set their hope fully on coming grace, live holy and reverent lives as the children of a holy Father, and love one another deeply from pure hearts.
section.frameNote: Three movements: set your hope and be holy, verses 13 to 16; live in reverent fear as the redeemed, verses 17 to 21; and love deeply as those born of the enduring word, verses 22 to 25.

units.label: Set your hope, be holy
units.note: as He who called you is holy

verses.text: Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance.
But just as He who called you is {{hagios|holy}}, so be holy in all you do,
for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”

units.label: Live in reverent fear as the redeemed

verses.text: Since you call on a Father who judges each one’s work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear during your stay as foreigners.
For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were {{lytroo|redeemed}} from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers,
but with the precious blood of Christ, a {{amnos|lamb without blemish or spot}}.
He was known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times for your sake.
Through Him you believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and glorified Him; and so your faith and hope are in God.

units.label: Love deeply, born of the enduring word
units.note: the word of the Lord stands forever

verses.text: Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, {{agape|love one another deeply}}, from a pure heart.
For you have been {{anagennao|born again}}, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring {{logos|word}} of God.
For, “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall,
but the word of the Lord stands forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.

hagios.gloss: Holy, set apart, belonging to God and reflecting His pure character. God calls His people to be holy because He Himself is holy, quoting Leviticus. Holiness is not first a list of rules but a whole life set apart to God, matching the character of the Father who called them.

lytroo.gloss: To redeem, to ransom, to buy back by paying a price. The word comes from the marketplace and from the freeing of slaves. Believers were redeemed from an empty way of life, not by silver or gold, but by the costly blood of Christ, so they now belong wholly to God.

amnos.gloss: A lamb without blemish or spot, the flawless sacrificial animal required in Israel's worship. Christ is that lamb, sinless and without defect, whose precious blood redeems. The image joins the Passover lamb and the sacrificial system, all fulfilled in Him.

agape.gloss: Self-giving love that seeks the good of others. Peter commands believers, whose souls are purified for genuine love, to love one another earnestly and from a pure heart. Because they share one new birth, love within the family of God is the fitting overflow of the truth they have obeyed.

anagennao.gloss: To be born again, begotten anew by God. Here the new birth comes through the living and enduring word of God, an imperishable seed. The Christian's new life springs from God's own word and shares its permanence, unlike all that is merely human and passing.

logos.gloss: Word, the living and enduring word of God through which new birth comes and which stands forever. Peter contrasts it with grass and flowers that wither. This word, quoted from Isaiah, is the very gospel preached to the readers, permanent and life-giving where all flesh fades.

basic.context: Peter now turns from what God has done to how we should live. Because we have such a hope, we are to get our minds ready, keep clear-headed, and fix our hope on the grace coming when Jesus returns. We are to be holy, like the Father who called us. We should live in reverent awe, remembering the enormous price of our rescue: not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb. And because we have been born again through God's living word, we are to love one another deeply from the heart.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the first big therefore of the letter. Everything commanded here rests on the mercy already described. Holiness is not how we earn God's favor; it is the natural response of children to a holy Father who has redeemed them at infinite cost. Peter grounds each command in a gospel truth: be holy because God is holy, live in awe because you were redeemed by blood, love because you share one new birth.
basic.originalLanguages: God who called us is hagios, holy, and so we are to be holy. We were not lytroo, redeemed, with silver or gold, but by the blood of Christ, the amnos amomos, the lamb without blemish. Having been anagennao, born again, through the living logos, word, of God, we are to show agape, love, for one another from a pure heart.
basic.typology: The precious blood of the lamb without blemish fulfills the Passover lamb and the whole sacrificial system, where a spotless animal died to redeem. The call to be holy quotes Leviticus, where Israel was set apart; now the church is that holy people. And the enduring word that outlasts withering grass, drawn from Isaiah, is fulfilled in the gospel that gives new birth.
basic.christ: Christ is the spotless Lamb whose precious blood redeems us, known before the foundation of the world and revealed at the end of the ages for our sake. Through Him we believe in God, who raised Him and gave Him glory. He is both the ransom price and the one through whom our faith and hope rest in God.
basic.god: God is holy, and He calls His children to reflect that holiness. He is a Father, tender and near, yet one who judges each person's work impartially, so He is to be approached with reverent fear. He planned redemption before the world began and carried it out in Christ. And He is the God whose living word never fails, giving new and imperishable life.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 19 gives the command Peter quotes, be holy for I am holy. Exodus 12 shows the Passover lamb whose blood redeems. Isaiah 40 is the source of the withering grass and enduring word. And Romans 12 echoes the call not to conform to this world but be transformed.
basic.oneStory: God has always been forming a holy people, redeemed by sacrifice and shaped by His word. Israel was called to be holy and marked by the blood of the lamb; now the church is redeemed by the true Lamb, Christ, and born again through the enduring word. The call to holiness and love is the same ancient purpose reaching its fulfilment in the gospel.

context.literary:
The passage is built on three imperatives that each carry a reason, and the reasons are what hold it together. In the Greek, verse 13 contains only one command, 'set your hope fully.' 'Prepare your minds for action' and 'be sober-minded' are participles that hang from it, so Peter's first demand is not effort but a settled direction of hope, with readiness and clear-headedness as its servants. The next command, 'be holy,' verse 15, is anchored by a quotation, and the one after, 'conduct yourselves in reverent fear,' verse 17, is anchored by two 'since' and 'for you know' clauses that reach back to the cross.

Verses 18 to 21 are the doctrinal heart. They are a single long sentence in the Greek, moving from what the readers were redeemed from, the empty way of life, to what they were redeemed by, precious blood, to the Lamb's long history, known before the foundation of the world and revealed in the last times. The sentence ends where the whole letter ends, with faith and hope resting on God who raised Christ. Hope therefore frames the unit: it is the object of the first command in verse 13 and the last word of the doctrinal sentence in verse 21.

The third movement turns from the vertical to the horizontal. 'Love one another deeply,' verse 22, is the only command in the passage addressed to the community's life together, and its ground is a second birth, verse 23. The passage then closes with a long quotation from Isaiah 40 and Peter's own comment, 'this is the word that was proclaimed to you.' That closing line is an inclusio of sorts with verses 10 to 12, where the prophets searched out the salvation that the gospel preachers have now announced. The word that was promised is the word that has been delivered, and it is the word that made them new.
context.historical:
Peter writes to scattered congregations in the northern provinces of Asia Minor, 1 Peter 1:1, and the memory his readers carry is a pagan one. 'The empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers,' verse 18, describes the religion of household gods, civic cults and ancestral custom that held a Greco-Roman household together. To walk away from it was to walk away from family honor, and that explains why Peter keeps calling them foreigners. Their neighbors saw not a new faith but a betrayal of what had been handed down.

To this audience the language of ransom was concrete. Slaves could be freed by a purchase price, and prisoners of war could be released for a sum. Money, silver and gold, was the ordinary currency of such deals. Peter's point is that the price paid for them was of another order altogether. Isaiah had already said of Israel in exile, 'You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed,' Isaiah 52:3, and Peter's readers, mostly Gentiles, are now taken into that promise.

The lamb imagery would have been familiar from Israel's calendar, even to Gentile believers who had learned the Scriptures in the synagogue or from the apostles. An unblemished year-old male lamb was the Passover animal, Exodus 12:5. Daily and festival offerings in the temple also required animals without defect. Peter was writing at a time when the Jerusalem temple still stood, if the letter is dated, as many do, before AD 70, so his readers knew what a flawless sacrifice meant and what it cost.

The Isaiah quotation also had local force. Grass in a Mediterranean summer withers in days under the hot wind, and Isaiah 40:7 ties that to the breath of the LORD. Imperial glory, civic honors and household status are the flowers of the field. Against all of it Peter sets one thing that does not wither.
context.canonical:
Three Old Testament texts carry the weight of this passage, and each one is taken from a moment when God was forming or re-forming a people. The call to holiness comes from Leviticus, where it is repeated at the beginning of the holiness code, Leviticus 19:2, and at the end of the dietary laws, Leviticus 11:44 to 45, with a reason that Peter keeps intact: Israel is to be holy because the LORD is holy, and because He brought them up out of Egypt so that He would be their God. Peter lifts that logic whole. Redemption comes first, and holiness is the shape of the redeemed life.

The Lamb draws on Exodus 12 and then reaches beyond it to Isaiah 53, where the Servant 'was led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7. Peter will quote that chapter at length in 2:22 to 25. The phrase 'before the foundation of the world' links to Revelation 13:8, where the Lamb is 'slain' in a book that predates creation, and to Ephesians 1:4, where believers are chosen before the foundation of the world. The sacrifice was not an emergency measure.

The closing quotation is Isaiah 40:6 to 8, the opening of the book of comfort. There the word of the Lord is set against all flesh, and the next verse tells the herald to proclaim good news to Zion, Isaiah 40:9. Peter's verb for 'proclaimed to you' is the verb of that herald. The New Testament elsewhere makes the same point about the word and new birth, Jesus saying that the words He speaks are spirit and life, John 6:63, and James that God 'brought us forth by the word of truth,' James 1:18. The word that created in Genesis 1 is the word that re-creates here.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wanted scattered believers to understand that the hope they hold has a shape. It is not a mood or an escape; it is a hope fixed on a future event, 'the revelation of Jesus Christ,' verse 13, and it makes demands on the present. The mind must be girded, as a man tucks up a long robe before running, and the passions that ruled the old life must be refused, verse 14.

He also meant them to hold two things that people tend to separate. They call on God as Father, verse 17, and that is warmth and belonging. They also know the Father judges without favoritism, and that is gravity. Peter does not soften either. The fear he commands is the fear of children who know the cost of their father's name, the cost of their own redemption, and the seriousness of how they now live.

Finally he meant them to see that holiness is not a solitary project. The sentence that began with personal consecration ends with 'love one another deeply, from a pure heart,' verse 22. A people purified by obedience to the truth are purified for one another, and the community of those born of the same seed is the place where holiness is lived out in the open. The instruction was written to people with no political power, who could not change their city, but could choose how they thought, what they hoped for, and whom they loved.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything here is command, but the commands are of two kinds, and the difference matters. Some describe a posture that follows from a fact, such as 'be holy' because God is holy and 'love deeply' because you share a birth. Others describe what the readers already are, as in 'you have purified your souls' and 'you have been born again.' The imperative is never asked to produce the status. It spells out the status.

That guards against two misreadings. One treats 'be holy in all you do' as a ladder: reach perfection and God will accept you. The text says the opposite, since redemption by blood is already accomplished, verses 18 to 19. The other treats the grace of verse 13 as permission to stay as one was. Peter says the former passions must not shape the new life, verse 14.

The Isaiah quotation is description, not instruction: flesh withers and the word stands. The application is to place one's confidence where it will not fail. Peter's readers are not told to pursue an earthly legacy but to trust the one thing that outlasts it.

debates.question: What does Peter mean by 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' verse 19, and why this image?

views.label: The Passover lamb
views.case: The unblemished year-old male of Exodus 12:5, whose blood marked the doorframes and spared the households, is the nearest model, and the theme of ransom from slavery in verse 18 fits an exodus frame. The letter also calls its readers exiles and describes their journey in Exodus language.

views.label: The Servant of Isaiah 53
views.case: Others point to the lamb led to the slaughter in Isaiah 53:7, which Peter quotes in 2:22 to 25, and to the Servant's sinlessness and the offering for guilt. On this view the whole sacrificial pattern converges on a single sufferer.

views.label: Sacrificial lambs generally
views.case: A third reading takes the phrase as a composite. Peter does not name Passover here, and the daily offerings and other sacrifices also required animals without defect, so the image speaks of every flawless offering at once.

debates.bearing: These readings are not rivals. Passover supplies the ransom, Isaiah 53 the suffering and substitution, and the daily offerings the sacrificial setting. Peter points to the whole system fulfilled at once and prefers the language of precious blood to any single source.

debates.question: Who is known 'before the foundation of the world,' verse 20, and what is foreknown?

views.label: Christ's role was planned in advance
views.case: The participle 'known before' means that God's plan to send the Lamb preceded creation. This matches Acts 2:23, where Jesus was handed over 'by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and Revelation 13:8 about the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

views.label: The Son's preexistence
views.case: Others stress that the One revealed in the last times already existed before He was revealed. The contrast is between a hidden state and an appearance, which implies a person who was there to be revealed, not only a plan.

debates.bearing: Both readings stand together. The plan was in place before creation, and the Person at the centre of it did not begin at Bethlehem. Peter's point for his readers is that their redemption was not a rescue improvised in panic, and that God's purpose for them is older than the world they live in.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 13 gives the first surprise, because the grammar is easy to miss in English. The only imperative is 'set your hope,' a single word with the adverb teleios, 'fully' or 'completely.' 'Prepare your minds for action' translates a participle built on the image of girding the loins of the mind, tucking up a long garment so that the runner can move. 'Be sober-minded' is a present participle from the verb nepho, to be clear-headed, a word Peter returns to in 4:7 and 5:8. The commands that follow are therefore forms of one orientation: look ahead, steady, clear, and stretched forward toward grace.

In verse 14 the readers are called 'children of obedience,' a Hebraism that means obedience marks their character as a family likeness. The verb for 'conform,' syschematizo, is the same one Paul uses in Romans 12:2 about being pressed into the shape of the age. The old passions were a mold, and the readers had come out of it.

Verse 15 carries the word anastrophe, 'conduct,' translated 'in all you do.' It describes a whole manner of life, the way one walks through daily existence, and it recurs through the letter, 1:18, 2:12, 3:1 and 3:16. Holiness is not a department of life. In verse 16 Peter quotes Leviticus 19:2, and his verb 'be' is the one the Septuagint also uses, a future in the Greek of Leviticus and an imperative here. The root idea of the Hebrew qadosh is to be cut off for God, set apart, and Peter's readers are asked to be what God is, in the way creatures can be.

Verse 17 describes the Father as one who judges 'impartially.' The Greek adverb belongs to a family built on the idiom of lifting up a face, favoring someone by how they look or who they are, as in Romans 2:11 and Colossians 3:25. Judgment in this verse is of 'each one's work,' singular and individual. 'Reverent fear' is phobos, and Peter will use the same noun for what wives show their husbands, 3:2, and for the manner in which believers answer critics, 3:15.

In verse 18 the participle for 'inherited from your forefathers' is a single compound word meaning handed down by fathers. What was handed down is mataia, 'empty,' a word the New Testament uses for what is futile and without result. The adjective for 'perishable' in 'perishable things such as silver or gold' is the same word used of the perishable seed in verse 23, so the metal and the seed are measured on the same scale.

In verse 22 'purified' is a perfect participle, meaning an act completed with lasting effect, and 'genuine love for the brothers' joins the word for brotherly affection with a word meaning without hypocrisy. 'Deeply' translates an adverb with the sense of stretched out, strained, as in 4:8. In verse 23 the perfect 'you have been born again' states a standing condition, and 'seed' is the word for what is sown, the origin of the new life. In verse 25 Peter's word for 'word' changes: verse 23 uses logos, the message, and verse 25 uses rhema, the spoken utterance that was announced, and the verb 'proclaimed' is the verb of good news.

typology.fulfillment: The lamb of Exodus 12 had to be unblemished and its blood was applied to the doorframes so that judgment would pass over the household, Exodus 12:5 to 7. Peter's phrase 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' verse 19, takes the same requirement and sets it on Christ, whose blood is not applied to a wooden frame but to the believer. The escalation lies in what it buys: not one night's safety, but freedom from the whole 'empty way of life.' Paul says the same, 'Christ our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The type falls short because Passover was repeated yearly; Christ's offering is once for all.

typology.type: The holy people called out of Egypt
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus 11:45 grounds holiness in the exodus: the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt so that He would be their God, therefore be holy. Peter quotes that same logic to people redeemed from a different slavery. The type pictures a people redeemed first and commanded after. In Christ the correspondence deepens, because the people now include Gentiles and the redeeming price is blood, not an act of power alone. Israel's holiness was often external, a matter of food and ritual. Peter asks for a holy 'in all you do,' reaching the mind, the passions and the heart, and the Spirit's sanctifying work makes that possible, 1 Peter 1:2.

typology.type: The withered grass and the enduring word, Isaiah 40
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 40 comforted exiles who watched their city lie in ruins, and it set the permanence of God's word against the fragility of human power. The prophecy looked forward to the herald of good news and the coming of the LORD, Isaiah 40:9 to 11. Peter says that the word has been proclaimed to his readers, and the herald's good news is the gospel of Christ. The word became a person, John 1:1 and 1:14, and in Christ the promised comfort has arrived. The type falls short only in time: Isaiah's word waited for fulfilment, while Peter says the word has now been preached and has already given life.

typology.type: Silver and gold, the precious metals that prove nothing
typology.fulfillment: Silver and gold appear throughout Scripture as measures of value and as images of tested worth. In Proverbs 17:3 a crucible tests silver and the LORD tests hearts, and in Malachi 3:3 the refiner purifies His people like gold and silver. Peter says none of this was the price of redemption. The correspondence here is by contrast, not by fulfilment: the perishable metals that could only buy a slave's freedom for a time cannot approach the cost of a blood that is 'precious.' The pattern of metals purified by fire reappears in 1:7, where faith is called more precious than gold, and so the passage ties the believer's testing to the Lamb's offering.

study.christ:
The passage places Christ at three points in time, and each one matters. He was 'known before the foundation of the world,' verse 20, so His work is older than creation. He was 'revealed in the last times for your sake,' so the long preparation has ended and the final age has begun. And He is now the one 'through' whom believers trust in God, verse 21, since He was raised and glorified. Past, present and future are bound to a single person.

The central picture is the Lamb. Peter reaches for the Exodus tradition, where an unblemished animal died so that others would live, Exodus 12:5 to 7, and for Isaiah 53, where the Servant is 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7, and 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12. John the Baptist points to Jesus with the same word, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' and the book of Revelation gives the Lamb a throne, Revelation 5:6 to 12. What the passage adds is the language of price. The believers were bought, and the sum was not metal but 'the precious blood of Christ.' Paul says it in other words: 'you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20, and 'He purchased with His own blood,' Acts 20:28.

The passage also shows Christ as the one who makes possible the holiness it commands. The call to be holy is not an invitation to imitate Him from a distance. It follows redemption, and Peter has already said that believers are 'sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood,' 1:2. The blood of the Lamb is both the ransom and the cleansing that renders the commanded life possible.

The resurrection holds the last link. 'God, who raised Him from the dead and glorified Him,' verse 21, makes faith reasonable and hope sure. A lamb that stayed dead would have been a tragedy. The Lamb who is risen is the ground of the hope with which the passage began in verse 13, which is why it can be set 'fully' on future grace.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The Lamb is a title of Christ, not a code for every lamb in the Old Testament. Peter's use is restrained: he says the blood was precious, the Lamb unblemished and the plan eternal, and he leaves the rest to the cross. The links drawn here rest on the New Testament's own words, not on loose resemblance.
study.god:
The God of this passage is holy, and Peter chooses to say so in the plainest way. 'Be holy, because I am holy,' verse 16, does not define holiness; it assumes that the readers know it from the Scriptures and from the exodus. God's holiness is not a rule He keeps but who He is, and it is the standard against which the whole of the redeemed life is measured. That is why a holy life is, at root, a life that resembles the One who called.

He is a Father who judges, and Peter does not allow the two to cancel. A Father who judged with favoritism would be a tyrant or a pushover. One who judges 'each one's work impartially' is safe for the poor and the exile and truthful toward the powerful. The believer can call on Him with confidence precisely because He cannot be bribed, flattered or misled, and for the same reason the believer cannot treat His grace as a casual thing. The passage holds love and awe together in one verse.

He is a God who plans. The Lamb was known before the foundation of the world, verse 20, and revealed in the last times. Nothing in the cross was an afterthought, and nothing in the believers' story was an accident. The redemption that reached these exiles was set in motion before the first day of creation.

He is a God who raises and glorifies, verse 21. The resurrection is attributed to the Father, who vindicated the Son, and this makes God the ground of the hope the passage commands. Hope is not wishful thinking because it rests on an event that has already happened.

He is a God who speaks and gives life by speaking. The word is 'living and enduring,' verse 23, and the same word that creates also re-creates. Against a world where all flesh is grass, the one thing that stands is what He has said, and what He has said has been proclaimed to these believers.

For worship, the passage teaches a particular tone. Reverent fear and loving confidence are not opposites, and a congregation that sings to a Father who judges rightly will sing with both. The only fitting response to a price this high is to live the rest of the sojourn as those who know what they cost.

crossReferences.note: The source of Peter's quotation, spoken to the whole congregation of Israel at the head of the holiness code. Holiness is not reserved for priests but commanded of the people, and the reason is given in God's own name: because I, the LORD your God, am holy. Peter applies the same words to a church of Gentiles and Jews.

The earlier form of the command, tied to the exodus: the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt so that He would be their God, therefore be holy. It shows the order Peter keeps, redemption first and holiness as its response, and that holiness here includes ordinary acts like what to eat and what not to defile.

The Passover lamb had to be unblemished, kept until the appointed day, and killed at twilight, and its blood went on the doorframes. Peter's 'lamb without blemish or spot' draws on this picture of an innocent life given so that a household would be spared.

Israel in exile hears that it was sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money. Peter's line that believers were not redeemed with silver or gold reads like a commentary on this verse, and shows that the price of freedom in God's economy is not paid in metal.

The passage Peter quotes in verses 24 and 25. The grass withers when the breath of the LORD blows on it, but the word of our God stands forever. Verse 9 then tells Zion to be a herald of good news, which is the verb Peter uses when he says the word was proclaimed to you.

The Servant was led like a lamb to the slaughter and did not open His mouth. Peter's Lamb is a sacrificial animal and also a person who suffers willingly, and he will quote this chapter at length in 1 Peter 2:22 to 25.

The letter's opening sets out the pattern that this passage fills in: chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, sanctified by the Spirit for obedience, and sprinkled with the blood of Christ. Verses 13 to 25 unpack each of these themes in turn.

Paul reasons the same way about the cost of redemption: you are not your own, because you were bought at a price. In both letters the price paid defines how the redeemed ought to live, and the body and the whole life belong to the Buyer.

The Lamb who was slain belongs to a book written from the foundation of the world. It supports Peter's claim that Christ was known before creation, and it shows that the Lamb's sacrifice is not a late emergency measure but belongs to the eternal purpose of God.

God chose to give us birth through the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creatures. It runs close to Peter's claim that new birth comes through the living word, and it shows that two apostles taught the same origin for the church.

John says that God's seed abides in the one born of God, and that such a person cannot go on sinning as a way of life. Peter's imperishable seed in verse 23 and John's abiding seed describe the same implanted life, which is the ground for the holiness Peter commands.

study.oneStory:
This passage answers a question that begins in Genesis 3: how can people who are dying, because all flesh is grass, be made to live? The fall brought a curse on the ground and a sentence of death on all who came from it. Peter's answer comes in three moves. The price is paid in blood, verses 18 to 19. The life is given by a new birth, verse 23. And the word that made it all possible is the word that outlasts every kingdom, verse 25.

The passage reaches back across the whole of the Old Testament. The command to be holy is the covenant ideal for a people that God redeemed in order to dwell among them, Leviticus 11:45 and Exodus 29:45 to 46. Israel failed to be that people, and the prophets look for a day when God would put His Spirit in them, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. Peter's readers are those on whom that day has dawned. They are redeemed by the true Passover Lamb and born of imperishable seed, and so they are being made into what Israel was called to be.

The passage looks forward too. The hope fixed on 'the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ,' verse 13, is the hope of the last day, when the Lamb is revealed in glory, not only in humility. Believers live between the two revelations, the one 'in the last times' on the cross and the one still to come. In that interval they are foreigners, and their holiness is part of their witness before the watching world, 2:12.

The new creation is where the word that stands forever finally stands over everything. In Revelation the Lamb is on the throne, and the people He ransomed 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9, serve Him. The grass that withered has been replaced by a city in which nothing impure enters, Revelation 21:27, and in which the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The holiness that Peter commands in an age of exile becomes in that city the ordinary air of life. What the exiles were told to be, they will at last simply be, and the blood that bought them will still be what they sing about.

quiz.q: On what basis does Peter command believers to be holy?

options.text: Because the God who called them is holy, be holy for I am holy.
options.note: Verses 15 to 16: God's own holiness is the ground and standard, quoting Leviticus.

options.text: Because holiness earns God's acceptance.
options.note: Holiness is the response to redemption already given, not the way to earn it.

options.text: Because their culture expected upright behavior.
options.note: The call is grounded in God's character, not social expectation.

options.text: Because they are children called to reflect their Father.
options.note: True and warm, though Peter states the ground explicitly as God's own holiness.

quiz.q: With what were the believers redeemed?

options.text: The precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19: not silver or gold, but Christ's costly, spotless sacrifice.

options.text: The sincerity of their own repentance.
options.note: Redemption is by Christ's blood, received by faith, not purchased by repentance.

options.text: Silver and gold given generously.
options.note: Peter explicitly rules out perishable silver or gold as the ransom.

options.text: A costly sacrifice appointed by God before creation.
options.note: True, Christ was foreknown before the world, though the answer should name the precious blood itself.

quiz.q: What does reverent fear in verse 17 mean for the redeemed?

options.text: Worshipful awe before a holy Father who also judges impartially.
options.note: Verse 17 holds together nearness as children and seriousness about holiness.

options.text: A sober sense of accountability to the God who judges each one's work.
options.note: True and part of the meaning, though it should be joined to loving nearness as children.

options.text: Cringing terror that God might reject them at any moment.
options.note: They call on Him as Father; the fear is reverence, not dread of rejection.

options.text: A casual familiarity that treats God lightly.
options.note: The opposite of the reverent fear Peter commands.

quiz.q: Through what have believers been born again?

options.text: The living and enduring word of God, an imperishable seed.
options.note: Verse 23: new birth comes through God's abiding word, the gospel preached to them.

options.text: Their own decision to change their lives.
options.note: The new birth is God's work through His word, not self-reformation.

options.text: Perishable seed, like all natural birth.
options.note: Peter explicitly contrasts the imperishable seed with the perishable.

options.text: The truth they obeyed, which purified their souls.
options.note: Related and true, though the seed of new birth is named as the enduring word of God.

quiz.q: Why does Peter quote all flesh is like grass but the word of the Lord stands forever?

options.text: To show that the gospel word giving new birth is permanent while all human glory fades.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25: the enduring word outlasts withering grass, and it is the gospel preached to them.

options.text: To warn that life is short so they should enjoy it.
options.note: The point is the permanence of God's word, not seizing the day.

options.text: To say that nothing at all in this world lasts, not even God's promises.
options.note: The opposite: God's word stands forever though flesh fades.

options.text: To contrast fading human achievement with God's abiding word.
options.note: True, though the climax is that this enduring word is the very gospel they received.

questions: Peter tells us to set our hope fully on the grace coming when Jesus is revealed. What lesser hopes tend to capture your heart instead?
Holiness here means a whole life set apart to a holy Father. In what one area is God calling you to look less like your former way of life and more like Him?
You were redeemed not by silver or gold but by the precious blood of Christ. How does remembering that price shape the way you treat your daily choices?
Reverent fear and calling God Father belong together. Does your walk with God lean too far toward casual familiarity, or too far toward fearful distance?

Because you share one new birth, Peter calls you to love other believers deeply from the heart. Who is one fellow Christian you find hard to love, and what would earnest love look like toward them this week?

translationNotes.note: Prepare your minds for action renders a phrase that literally reads gird up the loins of your mind, the image of tucking in a robe to be ready to work or run.
Be holy, because I am holy quotes Leviticus 11:44 to 45 and 19:2, applying Israel's calling to the church.
Love one another deeply translates a word for earnest, stretched-out love; some manuscripts read from the heart, others from a pure heart, with the same call to sincere love.
